utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hadzic, yesterday we wanted to show a video-clip featuring General Spegelj. I believe that you have to put on your headphones. This starts at the 41st second and finishes at 1 minute, 20 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] ... two or three men to get rid of the most dangerous ones. "Okay. "To get rid of them physically. Somebody goes to the flat. A courier. He appears at the door ... bang, bang, and goes down the stairs. "And then they can call the police and ask them who did it ... "Then down the stairs, goes to another one, and then kills him, that is, at the same time. The most dangerous ones can be killed at the doorstep. Never mind about women and children, none of that."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, you saw the first excerpt from the video-clip. Is this the video-clip that you mentioned in your testimony? Can you recognise the video?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the video that I spoke about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what did the general public learn about the video, who recorded it, how came that it was shown publicly. What was the general public told?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I didn't have any special information about that. My information was the same as all the other citizens had. We heard that it was recorded secretly by the military counter-intelligence. Rumour had it at the time - I don't know whether that is true - that it was Vasiljevic's men who did it. I knew that Zvonko Ostojic participated in the organisation of that recording, he was my colleague from school. Zvonko died tragically. Further on, you can actually see Zvonko's back when he was interviewing Spegelj, or talking to Spegelj. After that, when he was recognised in Vukovar, he was killed or assassinated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to start watching at 11:04.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Let's -- let's stop it then. Please stop.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah, I understand that. But they can't find the start of this -- this part of the video-clip in -- in the transcript. You gave a time reference, and they ask whether you could give them a page reference. Could do you that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh. It is -- it is -- sorry. It is page 5 to 6 of the English transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Page 5 to 6 of the English transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can we start now? Can we start again?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thanks. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] There are 9.000 officers in the 5th Military District at this moment. "That includes servicemen, musicians, et cetera. That's 9.000. And 18.000 soldiers, in Slovenia and Croatia and part of Bosnia. That means 9.000 plus 18.000 for the entire 5th Military District. And we have 80.000 men armed with Kalashnikovs. Let's say there are 10.000 of them with weapons ... "So why the hell did you go to Hungary? Couldn't you find the weapons here? "I guess have you no idea what's going on. We are at war with them. "With whom? "With the army."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does this video-clip depict Ostojic, does it feature Ostojic of whom you spoke?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He is the closest to us. He has darker hair than the other. The one who asked the other, "Who are you at war with?"

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now 12:21 to 13:30, also page 6.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] ... the commander of the newly established chauvinist forces. "Only like this. If a truck goes through Podravina and if the army would be alerted, then the president of the Executive Council of Virovitica should be immediately informed. And how are you going to do that, it's up to you to figure out, even if a child would have to take the message. So, if something happens, if a truck is stopped, immediately inform the president of the Municipal Executive Council. "One of these days? "Yes, one of these days. If that happens, it's better for us to know than not to know. It's not important where it comes from or whatever. "Okay, that's not important. "And we have mainly solved the problem. "Well, I've been having doubts about this ... fuck it. "Slatina is full of arms owned by Croats. "We know that."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, can you tell us if view of the date, 19 October 1990, did the Serbs know at the time that the arming process was under way among Croats?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't know it then. I didn't have any kind of information to that effect or at least people whom I spoke to never told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And after this video became public, what kind of fear did the information about the arming that was under way cause and the arming had been ongoing for several months? What happened between the moment when the video-clip was shown and a few months later?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was aired on the state television and caused panic among -- among the people. It had a dual effect on me. On the one side, there was panic, and the other side disappointment because I didn't understand why they decided to take up arms and against whom. That was the most awful thing for me. Those were the people with whom I communicated nearly every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So how did you perceive the situation? Who were the arms to be used against?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard on the video that they would be used against the JNA. However, since we were all military conscripts of the JNA, we realised that it was us, and because, under the constitution, we were all duty-bound to defend the constitutional order. The wounds from the Second World War were -- were all still open, and when you take into account, the situation was more than awful.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at 22:10 to 22:39, page 13 in the transcript. 22:10 to 22:39. Sorry, I didn't hear some remarks from the translation booth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you hear anything? Did you hear anything? Could you hear the -- what was said on the video-clip?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you repeat? Because the interpreter was speaking at the same time so I couldn't follow the video-clip.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] We are going to use all means, we are going to use weapons, and the Serbs in Croatia will never be what they've been so far, as long as we're here. Their supremacy is history. Their Knin is not going to be Knin anymore. We'll take over Knin. Knin is going to disappear. All Croats should mind this, and we will establish a state, no matter what the price is going to be ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you recognise the voice that you just heard?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I could. It's the voice of Josip Boljkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, in 1991, you communicated with him, did you not? Tell me, please, what was the option that he advocated? Did he ever say anything like that in your presence or the presence of any other representatives of the Serbs from Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had not heard this now, I would never believe that this was Boljkovac's option because he seemed like a reasonable man to us. His policies sounded reasonable.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we hear the part between 26:25 to 30:56. It's page 16 to 19 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the interpreters be given a moment to find the transcript page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Sorry, this doesn't work. We'll have to start over again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters just need a minute to listen to the tape and to be able to find the exact transcript page. You have to bear with us, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Sorry. You want to hear --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can we have the beginning again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: This was not on page 16, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, is it -- is it page 16?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's page 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I've got it now so we can start again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's start again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: THE INTERPRETER, Sorry, I'm still --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Yes, yes, when he throws him ... so they alarm Romic, he alarms the sabotage platoon ... "It all goes through the HDZ, indeed, and through its chosen people. The most loyal members of the ruling party are directly engaged in the actions of 'silent killing.' "So that's the group for silent killing? "Yes, exactly. The names of those who are in possession of automatic rifles are highlighted. Seven or eight men out of 17 are in possession of both automatic rifles and pistols. "Who's the commander of that group? "Glavas Branimir gives the instructions ... "On what's to be done? "Like I said last time, they received instructions on that from the bearded fellow from Zagreb, from Seks. "So he's actually giving instructions? "Well, look, I would say that is he an extremist - the worst one. Seks is an extremist and Vekic, if you ask me, is -- he is there only because of money. And Branimir is just a tool that they will get rid of one day. No one will even notice. "HDZ has made a plan on defying an order on disbanding and disarming of illegal formations. This plan has been made on all levels. The faulty imported weapons should be returned to the police station and not the JNA garrisons. "All those who are not Croats are suspicious. It's a normal thing. It's normal that those who are members of the Communist union are rejected automatically, that they can't be trusted. That goes for Bernardines, as they say. "What is the group for silent killing comprised of? "They will get instructions on when and whom ... from Branimir Glavas. "Where are those lists? "With Glavas. "How is the list made? "Well, listen, I've just told you how it's done in the police. I guess it's the same in the military. "There's nothing for the army there. It will be defeated badly. I'm thinking how to protect the two of you at this moment. Not from the army, but from the others. "Oh, fuck it ... "Every officer is covered with five men in Virovitica and they are all going to be executed while still at their homes. "We'll give you this list now, and you'll get the other ones tomorrow. "I must act quickly and tell those guys in Virovitica whom they should separate ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, this part of the footage was also shown on TV at that time; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What I would like to ask you, you've heard these words from Martin Spegelj and the whole conversation. Can you tell us, were these methods of liquidation really applied? Have you heard about that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I haven't heard that they actually succeeded in doing this because this was broadcast before they were able to. However, as far as Vukovar is concerned, in Vukovar, the liquidations of Serbs began before the war. I'm not sure if it was exactly by this method. I was never able to find out whether they actually came to the people's door and shot them twice in the stomach, but I know there were liquidations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were the perpetrators identified?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, people said that they were identified, but the authorities did not arrest them. The Serbs said among them that they knew who the perpetrators were but they couldn't prove it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the last excerpt. That's from 33 minutes, 40 seconds until 33 minutes [as interpreted], 33 seconds. Pages 20 and 22. Just one correction. Until 34 minutes, 33 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] ... possibilities. "This Ljuban ... village? "Yes ... "He is not defined ... "Yes, he is not defined. "And this one? "This -- this one definitely. "Highlight his name on the list, underline it. "Yes, underline his name three times. "Let them block him, don't let them kill him, fuck ... "Okay about that, but ... "Him as well? "Yes, yes. "He is not defined ... let's not say undefined, but rather frightened. "Should we do it to all of them? I can do it to all of them tomorrow. I can make ... "Everything, everything. "Okay. "And listen, a sergeant, a crazy sergeant that you don't take seriously could go to the barracks, prepare the forces and start shooting. "Fuck. "That's why they all should be ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Having seen this part of the footage, what is it about?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. President, if counsel would put on his headphones, he would hear that the interpretation is continuing. So we've really now got overlap between what's coming from the booth and counsel's question. I don't know that he said the video should stop. But I think it's really getting frustrating for everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry about that. Considering that this excerpt is 59 seconds, I would like it repeated.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] They're going to be killed even before they ... "And this one, Ljuban ... village? "Yes. It's ... "He is not defined ... "Yes, he is not defined ... "And this one? "That one definitely. He is the main one. "Highlight the last name on that list. "Yes, underline his name three times. "Underline his name. "Let them just block him, don't let them kill him, fuck ... "Okay about that, but ... "Him as well? "Yes, yes. "He is not defined ... let's not say undefined, but rather frightened. "Should we do it for all of them? I can do it for all of them tomorrow. I can't do it for all -- I can do it for all of them tomorrow. I can make ... "Everything, everything ... and listen, a sergeant, a crazy sergeant that you don't take seriously could go to the barracks, prepare the forces and start shooting. "Fuck ... "That's why they all should be ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, could you tell us again, how did you understand this part of the footage?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that these are direct orders for liquidation. They are making a list, who to kill definitely, and who -- about whom they need to think some more and run checks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We talked about this yesterday; namely, the proclamation of the Serbian District of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem on 25th of June, 1991. I would like to know when was this Serbian district established; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember well, it could have been ten to 15 days after that Great National Assembly because there were some more sessions after that that adopted this decision. This was just an initiative meeting. The Serbian National Council was the body that was supposed to put this into practice. It was the body that put forward the initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, 1D604. I would kindly ask usher to -- to bring the documents to Mr. Hadzic. May we see, please, 1D604.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Tab number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: 604. It's tab number -- just a moment, sorry. Tab number 776.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This text says that the constitution of the Great National Assembly took place on the 16th of July, 1991. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said about 15 days, and here we see that it was actually 20 days after.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it then that the staff of the Territorial Defence was set up, as we see written here?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally, yes, although we didn't have any control outside of Borovo Selo. Ilija Kojic was appointed. It was mainly an appointment within Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was this staff supposed to do in future?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was supposed to co-ordinate, if possible, with other local staffs. But at that time we didn't have either the technical or the physical capacities to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What do you imply by that term, "local staffs"?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the villages, there were no TO Staffs. There were local defence staffs in villages. So this staff was supposed to link up with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who elected people into these staffs?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were called village commanders. In -- there were different ways of electing them but it was mostly at popular assemblies, citizens' assemblies. However, in my village, it happened differently. They were elected at local commune councils. If was different from village to village. It was self-organisation within villages; nothing from outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: From what you know, was Mr. Kojic able to somehow integrate them, to integrate all these local staffs or headquarters, as you say?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was not able. I can't say that he didn't try, but he wasn't able to do anything. Because the villages had no communication between them, there were no telephone connections. All the roads where you do drive a car were not passable, so he was practically commander only in our own village. And, as far as I know, he wasn't able to do much during his tenure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see that on that occasion Janko Milakovic was appointed secretary of the Secretariat of Internal Affairs of the Autonomous District. What was this Secretariat of the Interior supposed to do? What were its duties supposed to be?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Janko Milakovic was elected at the proposal of Ilija Kojic because he was a policeman before the war, just as I was. The way I understand it, when I look back, there were two reasons why this appointment was necessary. One reason was that there were quite a few active-duty Serb policemen who had left the service and were still unorganised in this territory, in the Serbian villages, and they were getting restless and starting to make trouble, so formally somebody should have been placed above them. But the real reason was to integrate and restore law and order in the territory controlled by the Serb police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And here in the last paragraph, we see that you were elected again by the Grand National Assembly as president of the Serbian National Council. Can you explain to us why this was done, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember. That was the first time my position was officially confirmed so that I was able to start talks about organising a government. I don't remember, although Ilija Kojic says so in his book, that I was elected president before. Initially I didn't want to accept that position. And at this Assembly session on 25th June, the Assembly elected them and they were acting as a steering committee, but this was somehow more official.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: While we're talking about this Territorial Defence Staff, did you have any actual function or control over these Territorial Defence Staffs, over this one especially headed by Ilija Kojic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say "you," you mean me personally or me and the government?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I meant you, first of all. But you can also explain as far as the government is concerned.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had absolutely no jurisdiction over it, and the government didn't either, except for one short period when Ilija Kojic was also a member of the government, and that lasted until the two branches were separated and the position of commander of the TO and the position of the minister of defence became separate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the statement of Boro Savic that we've had occasion to see and in his testimony, he mentioned his encounter with General Radojica Nenezic. Could you tell us if you knew General Nenezic, and then I'll ask you follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him. If you can call that knowing, he was a very well-known personality in our parts. I saw him when I was 13 years old, before the war. That was the first time and the last time I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say he was a well-known personality, how was he known?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a national hero from World War II, and he was a commander of the Slavonia Brigade and later Slavonia Division, one of the greatest fighters and heros. And people said that although he was a commander, the commander of the division, he never told his men: "Charge." He always said: "Follow me."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Hadzic repeat the part of the answer after this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If you could just pick up where you left off after explaining how he acted in the World War II. And, please, a little more slowly.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He always went into attack first. He always led his men, and his command was: "Follow me." So he was ahead of everybody which never normally happened. All commanders stayed in the rear. I heard these stories as a boy in my village from my neighbours who had fought with him, and I also heard that he was physically the strongest man in the entire division, that early in the morning, during the morning inspection of all the troops, he would stand in front of his men and challenge his troops to wrestle him, and he said that if somebody managed to bring him to the ground, he would stop being the commander. He was an unusually strong man.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, you say that you first saw him when you were 13 years old in 1971. Can you tell us when it was that you saw him the next time, after that, and what were the circumstances involved?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He invited me to come to his villa in Belgrade. That was the summer of 1991. And I was shocked when I saw him. Literally he was half of the man that I used to know. He had had a stroke. One arm was hanging, limp. Also, saliva was dribbling from his mouth when he spoke. He looked very old and very sick. I remember well that somehow his eyes were hollow. His look was that of a person who did not completely have his wits about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that that was in the summer of 1991, was that after you had been appointed prime minister designate of the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem? Prime minister designate. To form the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was a couple of weeks after that appointment, perhaps a month later. It was in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how this conversation went between you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. His grandson was with him then. Maybe he was still a teenager. I'm not sure that he was over 20. In the living-room, on his table, he had a military map of Slavonia and Baranja and -- although I have to emphasise once again that this was in Belgrade, so 150 kilometres away from the war, and he talked as if he were in the war himself. Quite unrealistically, totally divorced from reality. From the conversation, I understood that he was expecting to go to Borovo Selo with me and to take over the command over all the Serb forces, and I don't know which other forces too. He talked about the establishment of divisions, units, Ustashas. I remember the bit about military security still obeying him but who were against him. This was an amazing conspiracy theory that he was totally immersed in. He even mentioned some security generals who were active in his day, this secret service of the JNA, who had been dead, and he said that they were still listening to him. I remember Brk Miskovic, Jevto Sasic, those were the names, I said they are either retired or dead. And he said: No, no, Brk Miskovic and Jevto Sasic, you don't know, they're never dead, they're always operating. They are dangerous. They are now listening to what we are saying. So I saw that he was living in a completely unreal world, and I regretted the fact that I had come to see him in the first place because that is not the image that I wished to remember. I tried to explain to him that I have no possibility of influencing the things that he wished and I am in no position to make that come true. All of a sudden, he started shouting, he got angry, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's just explain this a bit, if we can. You said that he called you and that he wanted to be commander of some Serb units. What did you mean? What were the units that he meant?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now, from this angle - at that time I didn't know about that - he wanted to be the commander of the Serb TO, as he had put it. Because he heard that Kojic was selected for that. It was probably after this piece of news in the papers. He then used an expression. He said how can this truncheon guy be in charge of that? It should be an experienced general, like he was. He said that he would bring his grandson along, too, so that people would see that he was not afraid that he might lose his life. So I found all of that to be absolutely insane.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you said that you could not exercise any influence there, can you tell us what it was supposed to mean?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it meant that I could not make those things come true, the things that he wanted, and that I did not want that. I mean, I found all of this very embarrassing. I suggested to him that if he wanted to, he could come and see people, speak about his own experience. He jumped up and got angry again. He said: That I should explain to a policeman, Ilija Kojic, he wouldn't understand. And, well, after that, I didn't want to make any suggestions like that. And his positions were 50 years old, if you will, as if he never lived in reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In what sense do you think that his positions were divorced from reality?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seemed that he did not understand that it was a new war. I had the impression that he kept thinking that this was a continuation of the Second World War, completely. So these were these Communist views. And the party that I belonged to was against that. So it was quite different. His thinking was different from the thinking of the people in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. Nobody would have accepted his ideas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly what all of that boils down to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these well-known pro-Communist views, leftist views. But of the extreme left, if I can call it that, that was totally remote, far away from the positions that I supported, the democratic centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If you remember, and perhaps you can illustrate this for us a bit, these positions of his, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I saw the state that he was in, I couldn't do anything serious. I just tried not to offend him in any way and to be polite. Because he was saying that he was faithful to the Supreme Commander, that his Supreme Commander, Slobodan Milosevic -- because he thought that I was in contact with Milosevic. Obviously that's what he thought. And he said: Well, there you go. If you talk to the president, tell him that I'm prepared at any time, day or night, to come and see him, wherever he asks me to come, so that I could convey to him my experience, not to Ilija Kojic, and if necessary, I can go to Pozarevac for a weekend. Pozarevac is the place where Slobodan Milosevic used to live. I said that I was not in contact with Milosevic and that I had no communication there. And then he was an a bit disappointed. And he said: Oh, how is that? And then he sort of calmed down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see that some words seem to be omitted in the transcript. So where was that he wanted to go? Who did he want to see?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wanted to see Milosevic. Because he kept talking about the wife of Mr. Milosevic, and he supported her ideas. Mira Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know which party this was, the party that advocated these ideas that he shared with Mira Markovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I know. That is the party that created the greatest problems for me in my life. That is the League of Communists, the Movement for Yugoslavia. That was the so-called party of generals, the party of JNA generals.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: After this meeting, tell me, did you see General Nenezic again?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him two more times. Ilija Kojic came once to see me, and he said that he had to go to Belgrade to see Nenezic because was Nenezic was creating some problems through some connections of his, and I wasn't aware of what that was then. And he said that he was supposed to talk to him and he said it would be a good thing if I went with him because I knew him. I went with Ilija. Then Ilija and Nenezic quarreled, and it was quite a quarrel. Nenezic wasn't attacking me anymore. He was attacking Ilija, and I was sort of a conciliator between the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it was that Ilija Kojic and General Nenezic quarreled about?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason was that Nenezic wanted to go to Slavonia and Baranja himself and he wanted to be in command there; whereas we were explaining that that did not depend on us, and we were saying that it was not possible for him to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So what did you say? Who did this depend on? I mean, if he were to go there.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We said that we were not able to do that at all. We did not have the possibility of doing any such thing, no way, these large-scale units that he talked about. He also talked about some bridge-head in Borovo Selo. That was the first time I heard the word. I didn't even know what it meant. And he said that if he came -- if he were to come there, he would command it as he did in 1941. He would charge. He would attack. I found all of that to be totally insane.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: After this conflict, did you have another encounter with General Nenezic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you describe that for us, that other encounter too.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was asked to come to Karadjordjevo to attend a meeting. And Karadjordjevo was a military institution. I didn't know what kind of military institution but in a way I was pleased because I thought: Finally, somebody is inviting me somewhere and I will finally have the opportunity of seeing someone. When I arrived there --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you just explain this a bit, what this means, to see someone. What was it that you meant by this specifically?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I meant someone official from the military. Somebody who held office. Until then, I hadn't had such an opportunity. When I arrived there, Radojica Nenezic was waiting for me at the restaurant there and another person whom I did not know. This was some man from Western Slavonia. We had lunch there. After lunch, we moved into a smaller room, sort of an office, and since there were only three of us, I found that strange because Radojica Nenezic said: I hereby declare this meeting open and I suggest the following agenda. I said: What kind of a meeting is this? What kind of agenda? I'm not aware of anything. And then this gentleman from Western Slavonia jumped to his feet and said: You cannot talk to the general that way. He's a national hero, and all of Gornja Pistana is with him. That's the name of a village, Gornja Pistana. Later I checked. That is a village in Western Slavonia with some 100 houses all together, somewhere in the vicinity of Podravska Slatina. So I said: What has that village got to do with anything? If they are with him, why doesn't he go there, to be in command there? And then he said: Don't be fresh with us. Don't you know that that village has been occupied by the Croats? How can he go there? I didn't know that the village was occupied by Croats. I did not mean anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you. Who said that? Who said that the village had been occupied by Croats?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That man from -- from that village. I don't know what his name is. I left and I never saw him after that. I heard that he had died. I did not hear it in time to go to his funeral. I would have gone if I had known that he had died. I heard it only after the funeral.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that General Nenezic arrived in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem after that conversation with you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did, twice, as far as I know. Once in a private capacity, he arrived in Borovo Selo, and together with another retired general, Jovo Kokot, they had drinks in the village tavern. He was one of the activists of that party, the Party for Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Could you please repeat the name of the party?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The League of Communists, the Movement for Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the second time he came, he was in Bobota village in a semi-official capacity together with a delegation from Belgrade, a delegation belonging to that same party, which included Boro Savic as well and Nikola Kaloper from Osijek. The latter headed that movement for Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that Nikola Kaloper headed that movement, what movement do have you in mind precisely?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Communist movement. The League of Communists, the Movement for Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened in Borovo Selo while General Nenezic and Jovo Kokot were there visiting the village? Did they communicate with anybody in the village or not? If they did, what kind of communication was that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in the tavern and they spoke to the locals who were in the tavern at the same time. Well, only drunks were in the tavern, but most of the people from the village were in the tavern and they spoke to them. And that meeting in Bobota --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Could you please clarify? It seems that it has been interpreted that the majority of the people were in the tavern. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. There were very few people in the tavern, but a majority of those who were there were prone to drinking. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear anything? Do you know what the topic of those conversations were?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, no. I heard that from my friends. I didn't have a service that could report back to me on things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And what about a meeting in Bobota? How did that go?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that from Ilija Kojic. They continued arguing. They almost pulled their guns at each other, and at the end, the meeting failed completely and it didn't amount to anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us why they argued? What was the cause of the argument, to the point that guns were almost pulled out? Who quarrelled with whom; do you know?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I know, people at the meeting were mostly the Serb policemen who had left Vukovar. I don't want to insult those people, however, they had been accustomed to having a safe and secure job. Somebody found it interesting that an officer came from Belgrade. They believed his words and his promises. Half them were on the side of Kojic, and the other half were on the side of Nenezic; hence, the argument. However, a majority were on the side of Kojic and that's why the whole thing fell through completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any other meetings with General Nenezic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never saw him again. May I be allowed to say something about that? At that time I didn't even think about that. I only started thinking about that when I arrived in The Hague. However, when General Aleksandar Vasiljevic testified - I don't think that he was a protected witness - he said something that I heard as a lie, I thought he was lying. And then, on the second thought, I thought maybe he wasn't lying. He said that I turned down their attempts to place trained officers at the head of the TO. Nobody ever asked me about that. I did not make any decisions about that. And then I remembered that the only conversation about that was with Nenezic and all the problems that arose from that, and then it occurred to me that that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The conversations you had with Nenezic and the fact that you were of varied political views, did that have any impact on the attitude of those people who were in the general's party towards you and Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem in general terms?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the gist of the whole matter. Nenezic told me: I know that you have a membership and people, and he meant the SDS. But he said: But you're powerless because all the power is in our hands. He wanted to contribute power and he wanted me to contribute manpower or people. But that was not a realistic prospect because I was not in charge of those people. I -- I did not command them. So all those who were close to those political relations and the Movement for Yugoslavia enjoyed a much better status than others in -- in view of Belgrade because at that time all the generals or nearly all the generals were members of that party.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now I would like to us go back to the situation that persisted in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem during the summer months and primarily during the month of July 1991. Could you please tell me something about armed conflicts and attacks launched by either of the two sides.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs were in their villages and in their settlements, and they guarded their houses there. There were individual -- individuals who opened fire on Serb villages from light weapons, and the army responded to the fire. There was also fire from mortars, to which the army responded. So the situation, I would call it, was a stalemate. There were individual activities and killings of some Serbs. For example, in late June, Simo Ponjevic [phoen] was killed in Brsadin. He was a civilian. It was unprovoked. There were several such incidents at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to what you know, do you remember if the then-Presidency of the SFRY introduced some measures aimed at dealing with the conflicts that existed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can't remember the titles and definitions of those measures, but those were decisions on disarming. The president of the Presidency, Mesic, signed a decision to that effect. Later on, all those who replaced him in that position did as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender previous document. It is 1D604.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D117, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see 1D762 - it is tab 783 - please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you remember if this is the decision that you just mentioned, the decision on disarming of irregular armed formations and on disbanding of irregular military formations?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the decision. And this is also about lifting the blockade of the barracks because, at that time, the Croats had already started blocking the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What about the barracks in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem and all the other military facilities there? What was the situation like with that regard?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember what I could hear and what I could read and see on TV. I did not have any personal knowledge about that. I know that in Osijek there were two large barracks. I had studied in Osijek previously, that's how I know. The military had to abandon those barracks and move to the Sector B or C. The Vukovar barracks was also under blockade and the blockade was stepped up gradually. Finally, the electricity was cut off as well as water supply. And in the media, I could see that that was the case all over Croatia in all of the barracks, even those where there were no Serbs. I thought that it was because of us, because we were Serbs, so that would prevent them from helping us. However, in Varazdin, Bjelovar, and Zagreb there were no Serbs there so no such problems could be expected, and still the policy was the same across the board.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the names of the cities that you have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just by way of example. I mentioned Varazdin and Bjelovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it is appropriate time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zivanovic. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Before I continue, Your Honours, I would just inform the Chamber that translations are completed and have been released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, we were looking at that document, 1D762. Can you tell us whether anything from this decision of the Presidency was actually implemented at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if later, after you got the mandate to make a government and after the Autonomous District of Slavonia, Baranja, and Srem was established and proclaimed, where were you based as the prime minister designate? Did you have your offices somewhere?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I didn't have an office or a car or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you spend your time? Did you live in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem at that time, or did you live in Serbia, like in May 1991?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My family were refugees in Serbia, and I usually returned in the evenings and spent the night with them. During the day, I spent most of my time in Borovo Selo, and if I was able to find a car, I would go sometimes to Pacetin, but that happened very rarely because it was not possible to travel. Whenever it rained, the road would turn to mud, and when the ground would dry, it was still not possible to drive there in a normal car. You needed a jeep or a four-wheel drive or a tractor. When I was in Borovo Selo, I was mainly in the centre, in the local commune, or in the tavern.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, did journalists and reporters visit Borovo Selo, both foreign and domestic press, in those days of July 1991?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to meet with them?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see the document 1D800, tab 793, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a story that was published in the daily "Politika" on the 13th of July, describing Borovo Selo as a men-only place. Is this a faithful description of Borovo Selo at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is because the women and children had gone away. They were refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see that foreign reporters talked to various people they met there, including some members of the JNA, but I see that you also held a press conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is on the page 2 of English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: What -- what did you say, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, yes, yes, I'll repeat. It is page 2 of English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says that, among other things, you stated: "We are in favour of a peaceful and democratic solution for this crisis, but it takes two to tango." Can you tell us what you understood by this? First of all, did you really say that; and, second, what did you mean?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that. And I meant that the other side also had to work for peace. It was not enough that one side wanted it. Since Croatia had proclaimed unilateral secession, there was very little room left for further negotiations. And we were in our villages expecting Croatian attacks. That is at least what I felt at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In this newspaper article, we read, among other things - it's in one of the subheadings - that there had been a truce in Borovo Selo for a few days at that time and the author explains it by the impending arrival of UN -- sorry, European observers. Were they there at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were, but I wasn't in that area, on that territory, every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: One more thing: What would your comment be on this paragraph that mentions your name and says that Goran Hadzic is the "president of the so-called Serbian government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem"?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll give you my comment, although I think this is self-evident. The newspaper "Politika" was the loudspeaker for the official policies of Serbia, and that was the opinion of the federal state and the Republic of Serbia about our government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see that just below -- I mean, after you, in the press conference, Ilija Kojic spoke, and he says that if the terror against the Serbian population in the area surrounding Osijek doesn't stop, it could be expected that people would mount a general insurgency. Apart from those few days of truce during the stay of European observers, had there been any armed attacks on Serb villages in the previous days, as we can understand from this statement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were sporadic attacks all the time, but there were two important ones in this period. That was the Croatian attack against Tenja village, and they had been completely encircled for at least two months.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would be very grateful if the other microphone could be switched off during witness's answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In addition to Tenja village --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Continues the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- there was also the attack against Mirkovci village. Mirkovci village was also -- was surrounded for two months, not Tenja. Perhaps even more than two months; I don't remember anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would tender this document into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D118, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Considering that your family were refugees too and had to go away, do you have any idea about the number of refugees in that period? How many refugees from Croatia were there in Serbia and in the district of Vojvodina -- the province of Vojvodina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you mention that period, I have to say that in the early days when the refugees started to flee, it was after this Spegelj movie was broadcast on TV. That was the first wave of refugees going to Vojvodina. The numbers were not large, but, still, there were quite a few of them. The major fleeing started after the events in Borovo Selo of the 2nd of May. Initially it was 10.000, and later, it increased to about 100.000 even.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you maybe have occasion to hear about the problems encountered by those refugees and how difficult it was for the state to find accommodation for all of them, to provide for them?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I just heard. I could see for myself because my family were refugees too. The problems were quite obvious but huge. Initially, everybody was prepared to receive refugees, but as time went on, and since it involved costs of food and accommodation, it became more and more of a problem. My family, for instance, had to move three times. First, they were in Kljajicevo, then in Backa Palanka, and then in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, 1D790.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is also an article published in the daily "Politika "on the 14th of July, 1991, and it says that in Serbia, 11.867 refugees were registered from Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. In fact, they were in Vojvodina. Is this consistent with the information you just provided?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But you should add, perhaps, 10 per cent to this number because not all of them were registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain why they were not registered?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of them had family in Serbia so initially it was treated like visiting family. Only later did it become a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D119.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we have 1D823, please. It is tab -- it is tab 800.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this text, the figure of 40.000 refugees is being referred to. Truth to tell, for all of Serbia, not just Vojvodina. Can you tell us whether, according to the information you had then, this did, indeed, correspond to this number of refugees from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You've pointed this out very well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it was not just from Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem but all of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you say from which regions or which areas these refugees came from? Apart from Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, we used to say the urban parts of Croatia. That is to say, Croatian towns. That was at the very beginning of the war or, rather, just before the war started. There was a lot of pressure in the towns, these silent liquidations, so people moved out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember which towns were exposed to such pressures the most and which towns had the most people leaving as refugees?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, practically all towns except for Istria and Kvarner, Rijeka, Pula, the area where the situation was ethnically more tolerant. So primarily Zagreb, Osijek, Karlovac, Vinkovci. Especially Vinkovci, all the Serbs from Vinkovci left. And, of course, the Serbs from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would tender this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D120, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how this situation evolved? I mean, this situation -- this military situation. What happened, to the best of your recollection, during the month of July in this territory? You mentioned the situation in Tenja and Mirkovci. Do you remember any other locations where there was fighting and where there were attacks?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember all of it, but I cannot really place all of that in the month of July. I remember the incident in Palaca [phoen], in Srvas [phoen], where there were liquidations of Serbs. Almost everywhere there were these individual incidents. The situation was -- well, as far as the front line is concerned, it was always the same. Everybody was at their starting positions. I mean both sides were. When I said "front line," I used it symbolically, because at that time there wasn't a real front line established yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned Vukovar in your previous answer, do you remember what the situation was like in Vukovar? Did you have any information, either personally or through the media?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember, from several sources, the Serbs left Vukovar, most of them, and especially -- especially the infirm, Serb women and children. Croatian children went to the seaside in the month of August in an organised fashion. Their party that was in power organised that, the HDZ. I remember something that could be indicative and interesting for this case today, the one that we're discussing. When these children were supposed to return to Vukovar, the war was already starting, and there were proposals for them to remain at the seaside, outside the war operations. As far as I was informed then, and later on I checked that, 20 years later, a direct order came from Tudjman that the children were supposed to be returned to Vukovar, and children were not allowed to leave Vukovar. This was written in Marija Krizmanic's book. These's a Croatian author. I read that book. I think she was a member of parliament at the time or she held some other office. In this book, she said that was absurd, and she asks what that was needed for. I also don't know what it was needed for. I can make an assumption, but I don't wish to make any assumptions here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to your information, at that time, could people enter Vukovar freely? Could any civilian just go there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the Serb side, it was impossible to enter Vukovar freely. There were barricades of the Serb -- of the Croatian police or, rather, this parapolice, the National Guards Corps. And Croats could enter freely through the Croatian territory that was under their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see 1D802, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask you now to take a look at this text: "Vukovar cut off from the world." It's short, and I think that you've had an opportunity to see it before today. At the time -- I mean, is this information correct, what we can see here, that, at that time, there were no telephone and telex communications with Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the reasons were? I mean, why there were no telephone and telex communications? Was that the result of some combat operations or was this something that one of the parties to the conflict did?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I look at this date, the 21st of July, I see that that could not have been the result of any combat operations. It was probably just simply a one-sided move on the part of the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would tender this document too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D121, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see now 1D763, please. It is tab 1446.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know that there were some conflicts at the time between the JNA, on one side, and the Croatian armed formations on the other?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know from the media. And, of course, where I was present in this territory. I was in Borovo Selo then, or in Pacetin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In this document, in this text, this newspaper article, there is a reference to the clash between the JNA and the Croatian forces by the Ilok bridge. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. My family was in Backa Palanka at the time, and I could hear the shooting and the comments on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us whether you knew, whether you heard about this conflict, why it happened?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say is that I heard that it was the Croatian side that was doing the provoking, but I don't know about any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would tender this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We object to that one, Mr. President. I don't think the witness has given a foundation for a number of the assertions that are made in this "Politika" article. Looking at the bold at the top, the aim of the attack is to draw the JNA into a conflict. Mr. Hadzic doesn't appear to be in a position to provide any information as to that. So if he wants to talk about a military operation or an event that happened down there, that's fine. But to offer the article as something that is truthful or is a truthful and full account of -- of what actually happened down there, I think in this instance certainly is not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I recall, although I cannot give the examples right now but the similar matters were used by the Prosecution when they tendered their own documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just to say, Mr. President, that any time we've tendered a document the Defence is free to object to it or any part of it. We're objecting to the part here that says that the aim of the attack is to draw the JNA into the conflict. This witness hasn't said anything about that. It's an assertion made in a periodical or in a newspaper, and we object to its being admitted for the truth of that assertion without there being some greater foundation. So we object to that part of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is my submission that this is on the Trial Chamber to assess the credibility of any evidence, including this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The truth of what is said in this document is something we will assess at the end of the day. The objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will become Exhibit D122.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, do you remember if any of the highly positioned state officials from -- visited Borovo Selo from the SFRY in July 1991?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember there were several visits. I was not always there. In the month of July specifically, the vice-president of the government of the SFRY, Branko Kostic, was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, P241. It is tab 190.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I don't think this is it, Mr. Zivanovic. Tab 119 seems to be a video-clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is tab 190.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see P241, please, on the screen, just to see what is it. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a transcript of the video that we already saw in this courtroom earlier today. You had an opportunity to watch it and to listen to it. Can you please tell us whether this is what was shown on TV after Branko Kostic's visit to Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when that happened?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In late July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know if it would assist my learned colleague, but I believe that we can access the clip pretty quickly if they actually want to play the video. I don't know that we've seen it today which was what was indicated in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I don't think we've seen it -- well, not in my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I -- I thought that we have seen it earlier. We saw it this video-clip in Prosecution case, not today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Or during the Defence case. It was shown here before it was admitted into evidence as far as --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just to say that we can -- if the Defence would like, we can -- we can put it up or if counsel just wishes the transcript. It's obviously in his hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it could be played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Would it assist?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm being told we may need two or three minutes, Mr. President. I thought it was faster than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Meanwhile, I could put some questions to the -- to Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, could you please tell us, were you there during that visit when Mr. Kostic visited?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have an occasion to speak to him personally, either you or somebody else from the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that Ilija Kojic was there and somebody else, and I was there, and we spoke to him. We will see in the video-clip who was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly what you discussed. As far as you can remember, what did Mr. Kostic say?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a courtesy visit, during which he said that he had arrived to see us, to show us that we were not alone, that we were the citizens of Yugoslavia, and he was the country's vice-president. He told us not to be afraid. That was the basic message of that visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It seems that the video is ready.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters have not been provided with a transcript of this video. Therefore, the video cannot be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: How long is this clip?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I believe it's -- it's six minutes. It's actually perhaps quite a bit shorter for the part that counsel wants, or what I believe he wants, Mr. President. We could perhaps -- the hard copy and -- or the transcript is in e-court obviously. It was up on the screens, but it's true that, obviously, the interpreters don't have it on paper with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I was a little bit surprised by the interpreters' reaction because, of course, if you have transcript, you don't interpret it anymore, you read the transcript, I would say. But perhaps I'm wrong. But six minutes indeed is long -- is quite long to do this on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We could skip to -- to play this video because it is already in evidence and so is not so necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. And you have nothing else to ask Mr. Hadzic about this video?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's skip it. Sorry about that for the booth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, can you remember whether the Serbian National Council approached the Presidency of Yugoslavia with regard to the crisis situation in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem? Did anybody from the council do that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ilija Petrovic spoke on behalf of the Serbian National Council and addressed them with this issue. I believe that there were several such attempts to talk to them. I remember that he would sometimes consult with me by phone, but most of the times he acted independently when he addressed the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we have, please, P192.140. May we move to the second page, please, both of -- in original and translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me, please, when it comes to this part right below the title depicting the situation in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, does this description reflect the actual situation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the following page in the original text and on the same page of the translation, it says that the police stations have confidential lists of the Serbs who had to be either be killed or arrested. Were you privy to that kind of information?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we knew that. We had that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that a judge of the municipal court in Vukovar was arrested although he enjoyed immunity as a judge?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I know, not only was he arrested but also beaten, if we are both referring to Slavoljub Sremac. But there were several such cases, his was not isolated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me about the month of August. You will remember that the attack on Dalj was mentioned here on several occasions. First of all, did you know anything about the preparations for that attack before the attack even took place?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know anything, nor did anybody mention anything to that effect in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, the 1st of August, were you in Borovo Selo or in the territory of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem at all?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was on my way to Borovo Selo. However, when I reached the border crossing on the Danube river, I could hear shots. I realised that there were more people than usually. I stayed there for a while. I didn't want to cross the river, the border, because nobody knew what was going on. And then wounded people started arriving. And then I returned with them to the regional hospital in Novi Sad to see if I could help them with being admitted in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, did you arrive in Slavonia at all, primarily in Dalj and in -- in the rest of the territory of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've just told you, I came as far as the Danube but I didn't cross the river. I didn't set foot on the territory of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem on that day. I did not arrive in Dalj for at least seven days after the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, do you recall that the Prosecutor showed you an interview you gave on 24 July 1991, where you said that Serbs were currently on the defensive but will move into an offensive very soon, much sooner than people think. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see P2987, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the beginning of this text it says that the inhabitants of Borovo Selo had spent another long, difficult day and that the shooting between Borovo Selo, where the Croatian armed forces were, and Borovo Naselje had been going for weeks and that tensions have peaked. Do you recall these events in Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It also says here that the postal services have seized to operate, as well as the railways, passenger traffic, and there are frequent blackouts. Was that indeed so at that time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It further says that the guardists have hit Crepulje, a border area between Borovo Selo and Borovo Naselje, with mortars and that fire had been opened at JNA members. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And it says that that evening in Borovo Selo -- in fact the previous evening, on the 23rd of July, the national council met. And on that occasion you said that the armed Serbs were still on the defensive but they will soon launch a decisive attack. When you gave this statement, what specifically did you mean? Did you mean a specific operation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I made a general statement because great fear reigned because of that situation which had been going on for a long time. I made a political statement. I said it's true that we were on the defensive, but we were definitely going to respond. And I meant the situation around Borovo Naselje because Crepulje is between Borovo Selo and Borovo Naselje.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you just repeat the name of that area between Borovo Selo and Borovo Naselje. It's not right on the record.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
