utterances.text: The part between Borovo Selo and across the railways up to Borovo Naselje is called Crepulje, C-r-e-p-u-l-j-e. There were constant provocations there from the Croatian police and the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was this a harbinger of some specific military operation to be launched by the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, especially after the attack on Dalj village?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. Perhaps my logic is wrong, but if I had known anything about that, I wouldn't have talked about it. Because it was a secret to me. I didn't know about it. If anybody did, apart from the army. I mean on that day, when I made that statement on the 24th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, in August 1991, were there any news about the situation in Vukovar? In fact, how did the authorities treat the local Serbs there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had almost daily information considering that I was on both banks of the Danube every day, both on Borovo Selo and on the side of Serbia, where the refugees were coming in, so everybody was talking about the victimisation of Serbs in Vukovar and the killings, assassinations. At first, people would say that somebody had gone missing, but very soon it became clear that those were murders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that in that time somebody from the Croatian authorities reacted to that wave of violence against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. I remember that a friend of mine, Marin Vidic, wrote a letter to the so-called Croatian top leadership. Marin Vidic and I were members together of the Vukovar Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, 1D275.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you answer that question, can you tell us if the news about that found its way into the media; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't say with 100 per cent certainty that it was reported in the media immediately. I know about that letter myself, but I don't know if I learned about it immediately in August or later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you look at this letter that I believe you've read before and tell us if this is the letter on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Direct accusations are made against Tomislav Mercep, who at that time was the secretary of the municipal secretariat in Vukovar, and his conduct. Does this letter faithfully reflect the information that was circulating at that time about raids on private apartments, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very faithfully and very sincerely. It was a nice surprise to me in the sense that somebody found the strength to say these things, to talk about it, even on the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that, as a result of this conduct, Mercep was dismissed from his job as secretary of the municipal secretariat?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mercep was very unpopular among the Serbs in Western Slavonia, and I heard that he went to Zagreb to take up the position of deputy minister for police. At that time, we didn't understand quite clearly if it was a dismissal or a promotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we can stop here, if you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We continue with this letter tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Hadzic, I remind you that you continue to be under oath. Court adjourned for the day.
